---
title: "See the model behind the settings"
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tinyAM)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = TRUE)
```

`plot_model()` connects a fitted model's settings to its biological components.
Choose a model above the diagram, then expand **Formulas and settings** to see its
actual formulas, initial-state conventions, fleets, surveys and age blocks.
The same viewer is on the dashboard's **Model structure** page.

These small cod examples illustrate two hypotheses. They use the same observations
and fixed natural mortality; the second adds variation in cohort survival,
recruitment and fishing mortality. They are teaching examples, not recommended
assessment settings. Warnings are retained, and no numerical failures are retuned.

```{r fits}
scaa <- fit_tam(
  cod_obs, years = 2000:2010, ages = 2:8,
  N_settings = list(process = "off", init = "exp"),
  rec_settings = list(process = "off", mu_form = ~ factor(year)),
  F_settings = list(
    process = "off", mu_form = ~ factor(year) + factor(age), mean_ages = 5:8
  ),
  M_settings = list(process = "off", mu_supplied = ~ I(0.3)),
  catch_settings = list(sd_form = ~ 1),
  index_settings = list(sd_form = ~ 1, q_form = ~ mono(q_block)),
  silent = TRUE
)

sam <- update(
  scaa,
  N_settings = list(process = "iid"),
  rec_settings = list(process = "rw", mu_form = NULL),
  F_settings = list(process = "cor_rw", mu_form = NULL),
  silent = TRUE
)
```

```{r structure, echo=TRUE}
plot_model(SCAA = scaa, SAM = sam)
```

The arrows show biological and observation relationships. They do not specify the
order in which the program calculates quantities. Teal nodes have annual
stochastic process variation. Setting a process to `"off"` retains the biological
component and removes its annual deviations. Initial parameters are a separate
choice; their uncertainty is not annual process variation.

For the SCAA example, separable fishing mortality is

\[
\log F_{t,a}=\alpha_t+\beta_a,
\]

and cohort survival follows the mortality calculation exactly. In the SAM-style
example, log fishing mortality instead has correlated annual increments, while
older-age abundance includes cohort-survival deviations:

\[
\log F_{t,a}=\log F_{t-1,a}+\epsilon^F_{t,a},
\qquad
\log N_{t,a}=\log \widehat N_{t,a}+\eta^N_{t,a}.
\]

Here \(\widehat N\) is surviving abundance, including retained survivors in the
plus group. The SCAA example estimates recruitment as annual fixed effects; the
SAM-style example uses random-walk recruitment. Both retain deterministic
\(M=0.3\). Full covariance and boundary conventions are in the
[population equations](../reference/tinyAM-model.html).

Adding `rec_settings = list(process = "iid", mu_form = ~ bh(ssb))`, for example,
would add a parent-SSB feedback arrow. A multi-fleet model shows the declared fleets
and their shared F blocks; total F is the sum of fleet F. See
[recruitment formulas](../reference/recruitment_formulas.html) and
[fleet/survey scopes](../reference/for_fleet.html).

The viewer describes a specification; it cannot establish that its parameters
are identifiable or its fit has converged. Inspect numerical and statistical
checks before interpreting results. A diagram remains available when a fit fails
checks because it only describes stored settings; its availability does not
validate that fit:

```{r checks}
check_tam(scaa, sam)
```

Common quantities are available directly as tidy tables:

```{r quantities}
head(get_ssb(scaa, sam), 3)
head(get_fbar(scaa, sam), 3)
```

`get_f()` and `get_m()` return age-specific mortality surfaces. `get_fbar()` and
`get_mbar()` retain each model's configured abundance-weighted mean ages.
These selectors preserve available uncertainty, units and projection labels and
do not calculate residuals or refit models.
